item.title: directory — who somebody is, and what proves them
item.description:
Who is somebody, and what can prove them? One model over a list held in memory, a SQL database, an LDAP server, or user and group blocks in a configuration file — and the point of it is the second half of the question.

go get github.com/go-authn/directory@v0.11.2

What proves somebody is not one thing

It is a fact about protocols. NTLMv2 (SMB) is a challenge-response: the client never sends the password, so the server must hold the password or MD4(UTF16LE(password)) — the NT hash — and an LDAP bind cannot authenticate an SMB session. A KDC must decrypt with the person’s key, so only a source holding the password can back a realm. SSH needs a public key. A second factor needs the secret behind the six digits.

So an Identity says which Credentials its source gave — Password, NTHash, Verifier (a hash comparison or a bind), PublicKeys, TOTPSecret — and Identity.Can lets a server say you can use WebDAV and not SMB before somebody meets a refusal at a mount. Each protocol has its own method:

answers from
Verify(password) anything handed the password the source’s verifier first (it may be an LDAP bind), else the held password, compared in constant time on SHA-256 digests so not even the length leaks
NTKey() NTLMv2 the published hash, or derived from the password; ErrNoCredential with neither
Derive(f), KerberosKey(f) a KDC, AWS SigV4 — anything that must possess the secret the password only; the derivation is the caller’s function
Keys() SSH authorized_keys lines
TOTPSecret() totp a column, or an LDAP attribute the caller names

The sources

package reads imports
directory a Static list, and a Set of sources in order the standard library only
directory/sqldir any *sql.DB, with your queries no driver: the program picks one
directory/ldapdir an LDAP server go-ldap/ldap/v3
directory/hcldir a users block naming a database or an LDAP server, and user/group blocks holding people x/crypto/ssh, hashicorp/hcl/v2, zclconf/go-cty
directory/ldaptest an LDAP server to test against glauth/ldap

In a Set, the first source that knows a name owns it, so a service account written down locally need not be put in LDAP. Group membership is the union of every source. Sources are read when a server starts; a password check may reach the source every time, because a bind cannot be cached without holding the secret.

hcldir does not decode HCL: the caller decodes the block and hands it over. It imports HCL only to write, for SetPassword. The build tags nosql and noldap leave a kind out of hcldir entirely.

Example 

package main

import (
 "errors"
 "fmt"

 "github.com/go-authn/directory"
)

func main() {
 local := &directory.Static{
 Name: "the configuration file",
 People: []*directory.Identity{
 directory.NewIdentity("dora", directory.WithPassword("hunter2")),
 directory.NewIdentity("eli", directory.WithVerifier(func(pw string) error {
 return directory.ErrWrongPassword // a bind against somebody else's LDAP, say
 })),
 directory.NewIdentity("svc-backup", directory.WithPublicKeys("ssh-ed25519 AAAA...elided... backup")),
 },
 Groups: map[string][]string{"staff": {"dora", "eli"}, "nobody": {}},
 }
 people := directory.NewSet(local) // more sources after it: sqldir, ldapdir...

 ids, _ := people.Identities()
 for _, id := range ids {
 fmt.Println(id.Name(), "password:", id.Can(directory.Password), "verifier:", id.Can(directory.Verifier),
 "keys:", id.Can(directory.PublicKeys), "from", id.Where())
 }

 // NTLMv2 needs MD4(UTF16LE(password)): dora's can be derived, eli's cannot.
 for _, id := range ids[:2] {
 _, err := id.NTKey()
 fmt.Println(id.Name(), "SMB:", err == nil, errors.Is(err, directory.ErrNoCredential))
 }

 // @group is expanded; an empty group, or one nobody has, is an error.
 fmt.Println(directory.Expand([]string{"@staff", "svc-backup"}, people))
 fmt.Println(directory.Expand([]string{"@nobody"}, local))
 fmt.Println(directory.Expand([]string{"@nobody"}, people))
 fmt.Println(directory.Expand([]string{"@admins"}, people))
}
dora password: true verifier: true keys: false from the configuration file
eli password: false verifier: true keys: false from the configuration file
svc-backup password: false verifier: false keys: true from the configuration file
dora SMB: true false
eli SMB: false true
[dora eli svc-backup] <nil>
[] directory: group "nobody" has no members: nobody would be allowed
[] directory: no such group: "nobody"
[] directory: no such group: "admins", in the configuration file

A held password also answers Can(Verifier): it can be compared.

An empty group, asked through a Set, is reported as missing

Expand refuses an empty group with has no members, as the second-to-last lines show for the Static itself. Through a Set, Set.Members returns ErrNoSuchGroup for a group that a source has but that has nobody in it (source.go:138), so the message names the wrong cause. The group is refused either way.

What it refuses, and why

  • A group with nobody in it, and a group no source has — errors, not empty lists: a configuration that grants nothing to nobody reads exactly like one that works. A source that is broken is reported apart from one that lacks the group.
  • An LDAP directory reached in the clear. A simple bind carries the password itself (RFC 4513), so ldapdir.New and a users "ldap" block refuse ldap:// to another machine unless StartTLS is set. ldaps://, ldapi:// and ldap:// to a loopback address are accepted. There is no switch to turn this off.
  • An empty password at an LDAP bind. In LDAP it is an unauthenticated bind, which most directories answer with success; ldapdir answers ErrWrongPassword without dialling.
  • Any other failed bind taken for a wrong password. Only LDAP result 49, invalidCredentials, is ErrWrongPassword. A connection dropped during the bind, a directory answering busy (51) or unavailable (52), is returned as ldapdir: the directory did not answer the bind: …, wrapping the LDAP error. The password is refused either way; what changes is that a server’s log no longer says wrong password to somebody who typed it right. Before v0.11.2 every failed bind was ErrWrongPassword.
  • Credentials in an LDAP URL — a URL is printed; BindDN and BindPassword are fields.
  • An NT hash that is not 16 bytes (ParseNTHash), rather than padding it into a hash that fails every login as a wrong password.
  • Derive or KerberosKey for an identity without the password. A verifier’s yes is not a key.

The NT hash and the TOTP secret are credentials, not hashes of one

Whoever holds sambaNTPassword authenticates as that person exactly as if they held the password; whoever holds a TOTP secret produces every future code. WithVerifier’s error goes to the server, never to the client.

What it is checked against

  • OpenLDAP’s ldapsearch reads ldaptest’s directory — the entries, the sambaNTPassword of the one person who has it, the group — and is refused with Invalid credentials (49) for a wrong password. The CI’s Linux lanes install ldap-utils; where ldapsearch is absent the test skips, as nothing in this module’s CI turns that skip into a failure.
  • ldapdir against glauth/ldap, an independent LDAP server, not a fake; the fixture allows the unauthenticated bind, so the test fails if ldapdir stops refusing it first.
  • sqldir against a real SQLite database through a real driver.
  • MD4 against RFC 1320’s test vectors.

The coverage lane fails below 85% (its stated standard is 100%), and the nosql and noldap builds are checked in CI.

Reference

pkg.go.dev/github.com/go-authn/directory@v0.11.2

item.title: ldap — the bytes of an LDAP server
item.description:
What are the bytes of an LDAP server? A library, not a daemon: the wire, the filter, the operations. authnd is the server that runs it and owns the configuration, the directory sources and the bind policy; this owns the bytes.

go get github.com/go-authn/ldap@v0.7.1

Written from RFC 4511 (the protocol), 4512 (the root DSE), 4513 (authentication), 4514 and 4515 (DN and filter string forms), 4526, 2696 (paged results), 3673, 4527 (read entry controls), 4532 (whoami) and 3045.

A Server is a set of handlers, each an optional field: Bind, SASL, Search, Compare, Extended, Add, Modify, Delete, ModifyDN, Abandon. A nil one means this server does not do that, and the operation is answered unwillingToPerform — not insufficientAccessRights, which would start an argument about permissions that do not exist. The root DSE is answered by the server itself, and publishes exactly what it honours.

Example

A server with one person who can bind and a search that writes what the filter matches:

package main

import (
 "context"
 "crypto/subtle"
 "log"
 "log/slog"
 "os"

 "github.com/go-authn/ldap"
)

var people = []*ldap.Entry{
 {DN: "uid=dora,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org", Attributes: []*ldap.Attribute{
 ldap.StringAttribute("objectClass", "posixAccount"), ldap.StringAttribute("uid", "dora")}},
 {DN: "uid=svc-web-prod,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org", Attributes: []*ldap.Attribute{
 ldap.StringAttribute("objectClass", "posixAccount"), ldap.StringAttribute("uid", "svc-web-prod")}},
 {DN: "uid=svc-web-stage,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org", Attributes: []*ldap.Attribute{
 ldap.StringAttribute("objectClass", "posixAccount"), ldap.StringAttribute("uid", "svc-web-stage")}},
}

// binder checks one password. A real one asks a directory: see go-authn/directory.
type binder struct{}

func (binder) Bind(_ context.Context, _ ldap.Session, req *ldap.BindRequest) (ldap.Result, error) {
 if req.Name == "" && len(req.Simple) == 0 {
 return ldap.Result{Code: ldap.Success}, nil // anonymous: the connection stays unbound
 }
 // A name with an empty password is an UNAUTHENTICATED bind (RFC 4513
 // 5.1.2). This package hands it to the handler, and the handler refuses it:
 // the comparison below does, since the password is never empty.
 ok := ldap.EqualDN(req.Name, "uid=dora,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org") &&
 subtle.ConstantTimeCompare(req.Simple, []byte("hunter2")) == 1
 if !ok {
 return ldap.Refuse(ldap.InvalidCredentials, "invalid credentials"), nil
 }
 return ldap.Result{Code: ldap.Success}, nil
}

// searcher writes each entry in scope that the filter matches, as it finds it.
type searcher struct{}

func (searcher) Search(_ context.Context, s ldap.Session, req *ldap.SearchRequest, w ldap.EntryWriter) (ldap.Result, error) {
 if s.BoundDN() == "" {
 return ldap.Refuse(ldap.InsufficientAccessRights, "bind first"), nil
 }
 for _, e := range people {
 if ldap.InScope(e.DN, req.BaseObject, req.Scope) && req.Filter.Matches(e) {
 if err := w.Entry(e); err != nil {
 return ldap.Result{}, err // the client went away, or a limit was reached
 }
 }
 }
 return ldap.Result{Code: ldap.Success}, nil
}

func main() {
 srv := &ldap.Server{
 Bind: binder{},
 Search: searcher{},
 NamingContexts: []string{"dc=example,dc=org"},
 Log: slog.New(slog.NewTextHandler(os.Stderr, nil)),
 // On anything but loopback: TLSConfig, and RequireTLS so that a
 // client that never asks for StartTLS is refused rather than
 // sending its password in the clear.
 }
 log.Fatal(srv.ListenAndServe("127.0.0.1:3389"))
}

Asked by OpenLDAP’s ldapsearch (2.4.28, as macOS ships it), with dora’s password in a file:

$ ldapsearch -LLL -x -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3389 -D uid=dora,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org -y dora.pw \
-b ou=people,dc=example,dc=org '(uid=svc-*-prod)' uid
dn: uid=svc-web-prod,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org
uid: svc-web-prod
$ ldapsearch -LLL -x -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3389 -b ou=people,dc=example,dc=org '(uid=*)' uid
Insufficient access (50)
Additional information: bind first
$ ldapsearch -LLL -x -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3389 -s base -b '' namingContexts supportedLDAPVersion supportedExtension
dn:
supportedLDAPVersion: 3
namingContexts: dc=example,dc=org
supportedExtension: 1.3.6.1.4.1.4203.1.11.3
$ printf 'dn: uid=dora,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org\nchangetype: modify\nreplace: uid\nuid: x\n' |
ldapmodify -x -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3389 -D uid=dora,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org -y dora.pw
ldap_modify: Server is unwilling to perform (53)
additional info: this server does not modify entries
modifying entry "uid=dora,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org"

(uid=svc-*-prod) returns svc-web-prod and not svc-web-stage: that is the defect, in the library this replaces, that decided it should be written. The root DSE does not list StartTLS, because no TLSConfig was given.

What it refuses, and why

A filter means one thing. It is parsed or decoded once into a tree, and String, EncodeFilter and Matches all read that tree. An attribute that is not an RFC 4512 §2.5 attribute description, or a matching rule that is not an OID, is refused by both ParseFilter and DecodeFilter: printed back, a “present” filter on the attribute !x read as a NOT.

Plaintext, when it was promised otherwise. StartTLS is asked for by the client, so a server that merely offers it has promised nothing. RequireTLS refuses every operation on a connection that is not protected, with confidentialityRequired.

A bind that failed keeps nothing. RFC 4511 §4.2.1: the connection is made anonymous when the bind request is received, and stays so unless the bind succeeds — so a re-bind with a wrong password does not keep the previous person’s rights. A simple bind with no Bind handler is answered authMethodNotSupported, and LDAPv2 is refused as a protocol error.

The handler decides what an empty password means

An unauthenticated bind — a name with an empty password, RFC 4513 §5.1.2 — is passed to the Bind handler like any other simple bind, and a handler that returns Success for it binds the connection as that name. Refuse it in the handler, as the example does. directory’s ldapdir refuses it on the client side.

A critical control it does not honour. ManageDsaIT (RFC 3296), password modify (RFC 3062) and cancel (RFC 3909) are named as constants because a client may send them, not because they are answered: nothing here follows aliases or referrals, so a critical ManageDsaIT is refused with unavailableCriticalExtension.

What an unauthenticated peer can hold:

default
MaxMessageSize 4 MiB a five-byte header claiming four gigabytes is refused before anything is reserved
MaxMessageElements 16384 BER elements counted before decoding: 4 MiB of empty strings once held 373 MiB before any bind
IdleTimeout 5 minutes the whole message must arrive in time, not its first byte; negative means never
MaxPending, MaxPendingAuth 100, 1000 operations in flight before and after a bind, as slapd’s conn_max_pending; one more is a notice of disconnection
MaxPagedSearches 4 paged searches open per connection, each a goroutine parked on its next entry

Filter nesting is bounded as well: a stack overflow in Go kills the process. Nothing logs an assertion value — a filter carries what somebody typed — only the filter’s shape.

There is no schema, so every comparison is case-insensitive on the value.

What it is checked against

OpenLDAP’s ldapsearch, in CI, and required where it is installed: the Linux test lane, the race detector and the coverage lane set LDAP_REQUIRE_JUDGE=1, so a missing client fails rather than skips. Windows has none and skips those tests. ldaptest, this module’s own wire client, is deliberately not the judge: it asks only what ldapsearch cannot, about one connection’s state — two binds on one socket, a SASL bind with an arbitrary mechanism, StartTLS followed by more LDAP.

FuzzMessage runs every message a client may send through the frame, the decoders and the filter round trip. The coverage floor is 99.7%, with the three unreached lines named in the workflow.

Reference

pkg.go.dev/github.com/go-authn/ldap@v0.7.1

item.title: kdc — issuing Kerberos tickets from a directory
item.description:
How does a realm issue tickets from a directory? AS-REQ and TGS-REQ, over UDP and TCP, with encrypted-timestamp pre-authentication required, for the people a directory knows and the services a keytab holds. It runs under authnd.

go get github.com/go-authn/kdc@v0.4.2

At v0.4.2 it requires go-authn/directory v0.11.1 and gokrb5 v8.4.4. The accepting half is krb5, and a service that only verifies tickets needs this module not at all.

Not implemented: cross-realm referrals, PKINIT, FAST, renewable or postdated tickets, and any kadmin protocol. Keys come from the directory and from a keytab, and change where they live.

Only a source holding the password can back a realm

A KDC must decrypt the client’s pre-authentication with that person’s long-term key, so a directory.Verifier — a bind against somebody else’s LDAP, a hash comparison — cannot serve, however well it answers is this the right password. A person whose source holds no password is answered KDC_ERR_NULL_KEY (null key), never the code a wrong password gets, so it reads as a configuration to fix rather than a password to retype.

Example

A realm in memory, on loopback:

package main

import (
 "crypto/rand"
 "fmt"
 "log"
 "net"
 "time"

 "github.com/go-authn/directory"
 "github.com/go-authn/kdc"
 "github.com/jcmturner/gokrb5/v8/iana/etypeID"
 "github.com/jcmturner/gokrb5/v8/keytab"
)

func main() {
 // People: a source that holds PASSWORDS. A verifier cannot back a realm.
 people := &directory.Static{Name: "the configuration file", People: []*directory.Identity{
 directory.NewIdentity("alice", directory.WithPassword("correct horse battery staple")),
 }}

 // Services: the realm's own krbtgt key, and one per service.
 kt := keytab.New()
 for _, p := range []string{"krbtgt/EXAMPLE.ORG", "nfs/files.example.org"} {
 if err := kt.AddEntry(p, "EXAMPLE.ORG", rand.Text(), time.Now(), 1, etypeID.AES256_CTS_HMAC_SHA1_96); err != nil {
 log.Fatal(err)
 }
 }

 // A keytab without krbtgt/REALM is refused before anything listens.
 _, err := kdc.New(kdc.Config{Realm: "OTHER.ORG", People: people, Services: kt})
 fmt.Println(err)

 srv, err := kdc.New(kdc.Config{
 Realm: "EXAMPLE.ORG",
 People: people,
 Services: kt,
 Logf: log.Printf, // why each request was refused; never a key
 })
 if err != nil {
 log.Fatal(err)
 }
 pc, err := net.ListenPacket("udp", "127.0.0.1:18088")
 if err != nil {
 log.Fatal(err)
 }
 ln, err := net.Listen("tcp", "127.0.0.1:18088")
 if err != nil {
 log.Fatal(err)
 }
 go srv.ServeTCP(ln)
 fmt.Println("EXAMPLE.ORG answers on", pc.LocalAddr())
 log.Fatal(srv.ServeUDP(pc))
}

With a krb5.conf naming kdc = tcp/127.0.0.1:18088 for EXAMPLE.ORG, the Heimdal kinit that macOS ships (1.5.1) gets a ticket-granting ticket, with KRB5_CONFIG=krb5.conf and KRB5CCNAME=FILE:cc:

$ kinit --password-file=STDIN alice@EXAMPLE.ORG < alice.pw
$ klist
Credentials cache: FILE:cc
Principal: alice@EXAMPLE.ORG
Issued Expires Principal
Oct 10 21:54:46 2026 Oct 11 07:54:46 2026 krbtgt/EXAMPLE.ORG@EXAMPLE.ORG
$ kinit --password-file=STDIN alice@EXAMPLE.ORG < bad.pw
kinit: Password incorrect
$ kinit --password-file=STDIN bob@EXAMPLE.ORG < alice.pw
kinit: krb5_get_init_creds: Error from KDC: no such principal in this realm
$ kgetcred nfs/files.example.org@EXAMPLE.ORG
$ klist
Credentials cache: FILE:cc
Principal: alice@EXAMPLE.ORG
Issued Expires Principal
Oct 10 21:54:46 2026 Oct 11 07:54:46 2026 krbtgt/EXAMPLE.ORG@EXAMPLE.ORG
Oct 10 21:54:47 2026 Oct 11 07:54:46 2026 nfs/files.example.org@EXAMPLE.ORG

The ten hours are Config.Lifetime’s default, and the service ticket ends with the ticket-granting ticket it was bought with. The KDC said why it refused each request, in its own log:

kdc: the keytab has no krbtgt key for this realm: matching key not found in keytab. Looking for "krbtgt/OTHER.ORG" realm: OTHER.ORG kvno: 0 etype: 18
EXAMPLE.ORG answers on 127.0.0.1:18088
2026/10/10 21:54:46 refused krbtgt/EXAMPLE.ORG: pre-authentication required (code 25)
2026/10/10 21:54:46 refused krbtgt/EXAMPLE.ORG: pre-authentication required (code 25)
2026/10/10 21:54:46 the timestamp does not decrypt (client etype 18, our key type 18): error decrypting: integrity verification failed
2026/10/10 21:54:46 refused krbtgt/EXAMPLE.ORG: pre-authentication does not decrypt (code 24)
2026/10/10 21:54:47 refused krbtgt/EXAMPLE.ORG: no such principal in this realm (code 6)

The first refusal of each exchange is the protocol working: the KRB-ERROR that demands pre-authentication carries an ETYPE-INFO2 hint naming the etype and the salt, and the client tries again with a timestamp.

Before v0.4.2, a till of 19700101000000Z got a ticket that had already expired

RFC 4120 §5.4.1: a till of 19700101000000Z asks for the maximum end time the KDC’s policy permits. Heimdal’s kgetcred sends exactly that. v0.4.1 tested only for Go’s zero time, so it took the Unix epoch for a real end and issued a service ticket that klist showed as >>>Expired<<<; MIT’s kvno, the CI’s judge, sends a real till and never met the case. v0.4.2 issues the longest ticket allowed, as above, and answers a till that has already passed with KDC_ERR_NEVER_VALID instead of a ticket expired on arrival (go-authn/kdc#19).

What it refuses, and why

At configuration (New): no realm (ErrNoRealm), no directory (ErrNoPeople), no keytab (ErrNoServices), or a keytab without krbtgt/REALM@REALM (ErrNoTGTKey) — rather than starting and failing at the first kinit, where the error reaches a person who cannot fix it.

At the AS: a request without pre-authentication is answered with the demand for it, and the person’s key is not derived until there is a timestamp to check, so a spoofed UDP packet naming a real principal costs no key derivation. A wrong password, a timestamp under another etype and one from an hour ago are all answered KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_FAILED, the code a wrong password gets; the error text names the reason, and so does Logf. A service asking for a TGT of its own is refused: services authenticate from a keytab.

One encryption type. Tickets and keys are aes256-cts-hmac-sha1-96 (etype 18) only. A request whose etype list lacks 18 is answered KDC_ERR_ETYPE_NOSUPP before anybody is looked up. With Logf set, the log records both etypes, so an operator can tell a mismatched cipher from a mistyped password.

At the TGS (RFC 4120 §3.3.2), a ticket is issued only when:

  • the ticket presented is a TGT of this realm, decrypted under the krbtgt/REALM key the KDC names — not under the key of whatever service the ticket claims (KRB_AP_ERR_NOT_US);
  • the authenticator decrypts under its session key, within MaxSkew;
  • its checksum is over this request’s body, as the bytes arrived, keyed with the session key (KRB_AP_ERR_INAPP_CKSUM when missing or unkeyed, KRB_AP_ERR_MODIFIED when wrong);
  • the TGT is not past its end (KRB_AP_ERR_TKT_EXPIRED), not before its start and not flagged invalid (KRB_AP_ERR_TKT_NYV), with no skew allowed: this KDC’s clock wrote those times;
  • the client is of this realm and still in the directory (KDC_ERR_C_PRINCIPAL_UNKNOWN).

Lifetimes. Config.Lifetime caps a ticket, ten hours when zero; a client asking for less gets less, and a ticket bought with a TGT ends no later than that TGT, so asking for krbtgt again cannot stretch a credential.

What an unauthenticated peer can hold: a TCP message, its length included, must arrive within 30 seconds; at most 256 TCP connections are served at once, and at most 64 datagrams are answered at once — one more is dropped, and the client resends or falls back to TCP.

What it is checked against

MIT’s own kinit and kvno, through pkgx, against a realm built in Go — no MIT KDC is involved, only the client is borrowed. TestMITClientGetsATGTAndAServiceTicket gets a TGT and a service ticket and checks the key version kvno reports. The Linux test lane, the race detector and the coverage lane set KDC_REQUIRE_JUDGE=1, and a further step fails unless the log says were served by this realm. The tests also pin the refusals a real client never triggers: a timestamp under the wrong key, one from an hour ago, a three-byte cipher, a service asked for straight from an AS-REQ, a forged service ticket at the TGS, and a realm backed by a verifier. The coverage lane’s floor is 80%.

Reference

pkg.go.dev/github.com/go-authn/kdc@v0.4.2
